newsitem.title: USA: Japan hard pressed to halt dlr/yen rise-US experts.
newsitem.headline: Japan hard pressed to halt dlr/yen rise-US experts.

text.p: Recent carefully crafted statements by Japanese officials should not derail the dollar rally versus the yen as long as doubts persist about Japan's economic recovery, U.S. experts said on Monday.
Vice Finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa voiced the latest in a series of delicately balanced remarks on Monday by warning that excessive yen weakness or strength is not favorable for the economy.
He said Japan will keep close watch on the currency market and continue to deal appropriately with excessive movements.
The dollar, which had briefly surged to a fresh 45-month high of 116.95 yen in Tokyo, retreated to trade just below 116 yen in New York after the Ogawa comments.
This modest dollar pullback, however, left some currency players unfazed.
"The dollar keeps going higher. It's just a pause," said Michael Rosenberg, head of international fixed-income research at Merrill Lynch and Co.
"I just think that the policy mix in Japan is a recipe for continued weakening of the yen," he added.

In December, Japan's cabinet endorsed a final state budget plan for the next fiscal year that emphasized cutting debt rather than economic recovery. An estimated increase in tax revenues was mainly due to a rise in the consumption tax, an end to special income tax cuts and expected economic growth.
"The fiscal restraint in Japan is going to be negative for Japanese growth. With growth already fragile, it means the (Bank of Japan) stays easy," Rosenberg said.
Japanese official rates have remained at rock-bottom levels, with the discount rate at 0.50 percent.
David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International Inc, noted that governments have three instruments to help the economy: monetary policy, fiscal policy and foreign exchange.

"The monetary policy channel is not viable in Japan because interest rates cannot be driven below zero. Fiscal policy in Japan clearly is not going to be helpful to economic growth," said Resler, referring to the upcoming tax increase.
"There is a growing realization that whatever economic growth Japan gets this year, it will come from a weaker yen," he said.

Ogawa's remarks echoed those of a senior Ministry of Finance (MOF) official in late December who avoided commenting on specific exchange rate levels but warned that Japanese monetary authorities do not welcome "wild fluctuations" in foreign exchange rates.

Eisuke Sakakibara, director general of the MOF's International Finance Bureau, who is widely considered the architect of the yen's decline since 1995 has also weighed in with his own finely honed remarks.
Taken together, the remarks have left some experts wondering about the real aim of Japan's currency policy.

Ron Leven, currency strategist at J.P. Morgan, said it is difficult to determine whether Japanese officials want the dollar rally to stop at around 116 yen or whether they can tolerate further gains as long as the dollar rises slowly.
"Both Sakakibara's statements in the last month and the statements overnight suggest that it's extreme movement rather than ...a level that they're focusing on," Leven said.
From a fundamental perspective, Leven contended the dollar appears to be nearing the end of its rise, but said it is too early to judge whether the dollar will make new marginal highs.
Meanwhile, Rosenberg of Merrill Lynch predicted further dollar gains. He noted that Merrill Lynch had conservatively forecast the yen would end the year at 120 per dollar.
"That looked bold back then, but now I'd say we're probably going to have to bump that number up," said Rosenberg, adding that he would not be surprised if the dollar hit 125 or 130 yen.
